newsitem.title: GERMANY: German wheat sales flat, buyers bide time.
newsitem.headline: German wheat sales flat, buyers bide time.

text.p: German wheat sales remain sluggish as domestic and overseas buyers held back, brokers said on Wednesday.
Export brokers raised nominal spot prices by up to 2.50 marks a tonne on the week, but said the move reflected freight and storage costs rather than demand.
"We're little changed from November when normally we would have slapped on higher fees to reflect costs for holding the grain since the harvest and interest," one said.
The Hamburg grain exchange lowered its bread wheat price (12.5 percent, 220 Hagberg) by 2.50 to 277.50 marks but maintained its spot feed wheat price free Hamburg at 270.

Brokers reported latent demand for first half 1997 from trade buyers, but said deals would be delayed over the extended Christmas holiday period into January if they were not arranged in the coming week.
Southern Europe was seen buying normal quality from France -- although the strike by truckers there hampered transport -- and Britain, rather than from Germany.
North American sellers also competed with Germany in world markets, trying to place high quality wheat for blending.
Domestic feed wheat buyers were covering much of their winter demand with British and Danish material, with the cif North Europe price competitive at 265 marks despite sterling rises.
Sentiment was also hit by the European Union's hesitant wheat export policy, which meant Brussels had not granted the volumes and export rebates traders had hoped for.
Normal bread wheat (12 percent protein) was offered unchanged at 282.50-287.50 marks fob while higher quality offers moved to 287.50-292.50 and 300-305 marks depending on protein levels.
Fob rye, although little traded, was steadier at 252.50-262.50 marks because of export demand and some buying by domestic stores.
Fob barley prices were steadier in a nominal 252.50-262.50 marks range, underpinned by demand from the feed industry and by a delayed maize harvest.
